title: Applied anatomy: the carotid sheath and nerves at risk in carotid endarterectomy

header.contentArea: Surgical anatomy: neck and carotid surgery

brief.scenario: Mr Duncan Hawksworth, 72, had 20 minutes of left arm weakness and slurred speech four days ago. Carotid duplex shows a severe right internal carotid artery stenosis. He is listed for right carotid endarterectomy.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the structures met during the exposure, the carotid sheath, the nerves at risk and the criteria for surgery.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Sheath, then exposure, then nerves and deficits, then who qualifies and how soon.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Putting the external carotid in the sheath, or quoting a stenosis figure without saying NASCET or ECST.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "The sheath contains the common and internal carotid arteries, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve."

grid.label: Carotid sheath contents
grid.fail: Cannot name the contents, or places the external carotid artery or sympathetic trunk inside the sheath.
grid.pass: Common and internal carotid arteries, internal jugular vein laterally, vagus nerve posteriorly between them.
grid.high: Adds that all three layers of deep cervical fascia contribute, ansa cervicalis lies on it and the sympathetic trunk lies behind it.

grid.label: Describes the structures met in the exposure
grid.fail: Cannot describe the structures met, or omits the internal jugular vein or the hypoglossal nerve.
grid.pass: Describes sternocleidomastoid retracted, internal jugular vein, common facial vein, carotid bifurcation, internal and external carotids, and the hypoglossal nerve crossing them.
grid.high: Tells the carotids apart by branches (external has them, internal has none in the neck) and describes ansa cervicalis descending from the hypoglossal.

grid.label: Nerves at risk and deficits
grid.fail: Names only the facial nerve, or cannot give a deficit for any nerve.
grid.pass: Hypoglossal (tongue deviates to the injured side), vagus or recurrent laryngeal (hoarseness), marginal mandibular (lower lip asymmetry).
grid.high: Adds superior laryngeal (voice fatigue, lost high pitch), glossopharyngeal in high dissection (dysphagia) and greater auricular (numb earlobe).

grid.label: Criteria for surgery
grid.fail: Cannot give a threshold, or gives a percentage without the measurement method.
grid.pass: Symptomatic stenosis 50 to 99% NASCET or 70 to 99% ECST, with stable symptoms after TIA or non-disabling stroke, plus best medical treatment.
grid.high: Below those thresholds: no surgery, best medical treatment. Imaging reports must state which criteria were used.

grid.label: Timing
grid.fail: Says surgery can wait for a routine list.
grid.pass: Urgent referral; surgery as soon as possible and within 1 week of first presentation.
grid.high: Explains that recurrent stroke risk is highest in the first days, so the benefit of surgery falls with delay.

grid.label: NASCET versus ECST
grid.fail: Cannot explain how the two methods differ.
grid.pass: NASCET compares the residual lumen with the normal distal internal carotid; ECST with the estimated original bulb diameter.
grid.high: ECST gives the higher figure for the same stenosis, which is why the paired thresholds differ.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What does the carotid sheath contain?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The carotid arteries, including the external carotid, and the sympathetic chain.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Through an incision along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, describe the structures you meet as you expose the carotid bifurcation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The jugular vein, I think, and then the carotid. I'm not sure which nerves cross it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's severe, so yes. Anything over 70% needs an operation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: On the next routine list after the clinic letter.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: On the duplex. I'm not sure what NASCET means.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Through an incision along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, describe the structures you meet as you expose the carotid bifurcation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Sternocleidomastoid is retracted, then the internal jugular vein and the common facial vein, then the bifurcation with internal and external carotids, and the hypoglossal nerve crossing them.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Common and internal carotid arteries, the internal jugular vein laterally and the vagus nerve posteriorly between them.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hypoglossal: tongue deviates to the injured side. Vagus or recurrent laryngeal: hoarseness. Marginal mandibular: lower lip asymmetry.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes if it's 50 to 99% NASCET, or 70 to 99% ECST, with best medical treatment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgently: as soon as possible and within a week of presentation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: NASCET compares the residual lumen with normal distal internal carotid. ECST uses the estimated original diameter of the bulb.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Through an incision along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, describe the structures you meet as you expose the carotid bifurcation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Internal jugular vein, common facial vein, the bifurcation, and the hypoglossal nerve crossing both carotids. The external carotid has branches, such as the superior thyroid; the internal has none in the neck. Ansa cervicalis descends from the hypoglossal.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: All three layers of deep cervical fascia contribute. It holds the common and internal carotids, internal jugular vein and vagus. Ansa cervicalis lies on it; the sympathetic trunk lies behind it, outside.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Beyond hypoglossal, vagus and marginal mandibular: superior laryngeal, giving voice fatigue and lost high pitch; glossopharyngeal in a high dissection, with dysphagia; and greater auricular, a numb earlobe.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd ask which method. 60% NASCET qualifies; 60% ECST is below 70%, so best medical treatment only. Reports must state the criteria.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Recurrent stroke risk is highest in the first days, so the benefit falls with delay.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: ECST measures against the bulb, which is wider, so it gives the higher figure for the same stenosis.

failures.move: Placing the external carotid or sympathetic trunk inside the sheath.
failures.consequence: The anatomy of the exposure is wrong from the start.
The nerve crossing the operative field is missed, and so is its deficit.

failures.move: Quoting a percentage without NASCET or ECST.
failures.consequence: The same stenosis can qualify or not depending on the method.
He stays exposed to early recurrent stroke while waiting.

recovery.when: You can't tell the internal from the external carotid
recovery.line: The external carotid has branches in the neck; the internal has none.
I'd want to know whether that is NASCET or ECST before deciding.

knowledge.fact: Sheath: common and internal carotid, internal jugular vein, vagus. Sympathetic trunk lies behind it.
Hypoglossal nerve crosses superficial to both carotids above the bifurcation; ansa cervicalis descends from it.
Endarterectomy: symptomatic 50 to 99% NASCET or 70 to 99% ECST, with best medical treatment. Below that, no surgery. Reports state the criteria.
Operate as soon as possible and within 1 week of first presentation.

recall.think: Recurrent stroke in the days after a TIA.
recall.say: "50 to 99% NASCET: urgent endarterectomy with best medical treatment."
do: Name hypoglossal, vagus and marginal mandibular with deficits
recall.trap: A bare percentage with no method.
recall.finish: Urgent endarterectomy, nerves identified and protected.

push.question: What does the carotid sheath contain?
push.expect: Common and internal carotid, internal jugular vein, vagus.

push.question: Which nerves are at risk, and what happens if each is injured?
push.expect: Hypoglossal, vagus or recurrent laryngeal, marginal mandibular, with deficits.

push.question: Does he meet the criteria for surgery, and how soon?
push.expect: Yes at 50-99% NASCET; within 1 week of presentation.

push.question: How do NASCET and ECST differ?
push.expect: Distal internal carotid versus estimated bulb diameter; ECST reads higher.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Asks which method: qualifies if NASCET, not if ECST.

curveballs.prompt: At operation, how do you tell the external carotid from the internal?
curveballs.safeAnswer: The one with branches in the neck, such as the superior thyroid artery.

curveballs.prompt: After surgery his tongue deviates to the right on protrusion.
